finding.claim: SQL injection in /search: the raw `q` query parameter is interpolated into an f-string SQL LIKE clause, letting an unauthenticated attacker break out of the string literal and append arbitrary SELECT clauses (e.g. UNION) to read any table in shop.db.
finding.source: request.args.get("q") at app.py:11 (unauthenticated HTTP query string)
finding.sink: db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'") at app.py:12

trace.note: term = request.args.get("q", "") — attacker-controlled, no validation or length/charset check
f-string concatenates term directly into the SQL text; a single quote closes the LIKE literal
db.execute runs the attacker-shaped SQL on the shared sqlite3 connection; e.g. q=x' UNION SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master-- returns schema, and UNION SELECT over other tables returns their rows
fetchall rows returned to the caller via jsonify, so UNION results are exfiltrated directly in the HTTP response

finding.guards_checked: No parameter binding on this query (f-string used instead of ? placeholder). No input validation, escaping, allowlist or length limit on `q`. No authentication or authorization decorator on the route. Partial natural limit only: sqlite3.execute rejects multiple statements, so stacked writes (e.g. DROP/UPDATE) are blocked, but UNION-based and boolean-based read injection are not. The column count must match (2 columns) for UNION, which is easy to satisfy by inspection of the SELECT list. Not present: `%` in LIKE is not escaped, which is a minor wildcard issue on top of the injection.

verdict.guard_found: none. The route at app.py:9-10 has no auth decorator. The value from request.args.get("q") at app.py:11 is interpolated into the f-string SQL at app.py:12 with no parameter binding, escaping, allowlist, or length check. sqlite3's single-statement limit blocks stacked writes but not UNION-based reads, and the fetchall result is returned via jsonify at app.py:13.
verdict.reason: The attacker is anonymous, the f-string at app.py:12 splices the unvalidated `term` from app.py:11 straight into SQL, and the rows come back through jsonify at app.py:13, so UNION-based reads of other tables work; the candidate's trace matches the file exactly.

finding.claim: Possible unauthenticated enumeration of product listings by owner: /by-owner returns product ids and names for any caller-supplied owner value with no authentication or ownership check. This is a finding only if product-to-owner association is meant to be private. Parameter binding here prevents SQL injection but does not address authorization.
finding.source: request.args.get("owner", "") at app.py:24 (unauthenticated HTTP query string)
finding.sink: db.execute("SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE owner = ?", (owner,)) at app.py:25, returning owner-filtered listings via jsonify at app.py:26

trace.note: owner = request.args.get("owner", "") — attacker chooses any owner identifier, including the empty string
owner passed as a bound parameter to the owner-filtered SELECT; no injection, but the query returns all products belonging to that owner
matching id/name pairs returned to any anonymous caller; the route has no session, token, or tenant check

finding.guards_checked: Parameterized query (prevents SQL injection at line 25). No authentication decorator, session check, or caller-identity comparison against `owner` anywhere in app.py. No restriction on which owner values can be queried. Whether this is a vulnerability depends on business intent for the owner column, which is not visible in this file. The /product/<int:pid> route at app.py:16-19 was checked and is not reported: it is parameterized with an int converter and does not return the owner column.

verdict.guard_found: Parameterized query at app.py:25 (blocks SQL injection only). No authentication, session, or owner-identity check anywhere in app.py. The only other route (/product/<int:pid>, app.py:16-19) does not return owner.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: app.py:24 takes an arbitrary `owner` from the query string, app.py:25 binds it into an owner-filtered SELECT, and app.py:26 returns id/name pairs to an anonymous caller with no check. Whether this is a vulnerability depends on whether product-to-owner mapping is meant to be private, which this file cannot show. The app also exposes all products publicly via /search (app.py:9-13), so unauthenticated listing may be intended.
